That is, it brings good tidings to the people of obedience and warns the people of disobedience. ﴿But most of them turned away﴾ from reflecting upon it, although it is in their own language.

﴿So they do not hear﴾ with the hearing of contemplation and reflection, such that they would comprehend its great worth and believe in it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 41, verse 5:

﴿And they said﴾ (p-3) That is, to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, when he called them to faith and to acting upon what is in the Qur'an.

﴿Our hearts are in coverings﴾ That is, in veils.

﴿from what you call us to, and in our ears is a deafness﴾ That is, a deafness of heaviness (ṣamam al-thiql). It is also read with a kasra (on the wāw, wiqr), and it is read with a fatḥa on the qāf (waqr).

﴿and between us and you there is a barrier﴾ a thick one, which prevents us from communicating. The "min" (from) indicates that the barrier originates from both sides, such that it fills the intervening distance entirely, so that no gap at all remains between them. These are images depicting the dullness of their hearts to perceive and accept the truth, their ears rejecting it as though there were deafness in them, and their refusal to connect with or agree with the Messenger ﷺ.

﴿So act﴾ That is, according to your religion. It has also been said: work to nullify our affair.

﴿Indeed, we are acting﴾ That is, according to our religion. It has also been said: working to nullify your affair. The first is the more apparent.

Indeed, His saying, ﴿Say: I am only a human being like you, to whom it is revealed that your God is one God﴾, is a prompt for the answer to them. That is: I am not of a different kind from you, such that there would be between me and you a barrier and a difference that justifies the difference in deeds and religions, as your saying indicates: ﴿Then act, for we are acting﴾. Rather, I am like you, commanded with what you are commanded, since we have all been informed of the tawhid (the affirmation of God's oneness) in a comprehensive address that includes me and you. The address in "your God" is reported speech that encompasses everyone, not an address from him, peace and blessings be upon him, to the disbelievers, as in "like you" (mithlukum).

It has also been said: the meaning is, I am not an angel nor a jinn, such that you could not receive from him, and I do not call you to what minds and ears recoil from; rather, I call you to tawhid and to uprightness (istiqamah) in action. Both are indicated by the evidences of reason and the testimonies of transmitted revelation.

It has also been said: the meaning is, I am not an angel; I am only a human being like you, and it has been revealed to me without you. The validity of my prophethood is established by the revelation given to me, while I am a human being. When my prophethood is valid, it becomes obligatory upon you to follow me. So reflect.

As for the fa' (the particle "so") in His saying, ﴿So take the straight path to Him﴾ (fastaqimu), it marks the sequence of what follows upon what precedes, namely the revival of the oneness of God, for that necessitates their uprightness toward Him, exalted is He, through tawhid and sincerity in their deeds.

﴿And seek His forgiveness﴾ for what you were upon of bad belief and bad conduct. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And woe to the polytheists﴾, is a warning and a deterrent against shirk, following their encouragement toward tawhid.

Abu al-Su'ud's commentary (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 41, verse 7:

He described them with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those who do not give the zakat﴾, to intensify the warning and the frightening against withholding zakat, since it is made one of the attributes of the polytheists and is coupled with disbelief in the Hereafter, where He said: ﴿and they, in the Hereafter, are disbelievers﴾. This is a conjunction with "do not give" (la yu'tuna), and it falls within the scope of the relative clause. The difference between the two in being verbal and nominal is because their not giving is renewed (mutajaddid), whereas disbelief is a continuous matter (amr mustamirr). It is transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that he interpreted "do not give the zakat" with his saying: "They do not say, there is no god but Allah, for it is the zakat of the souls (zakat al-anfus)." The meaning is: they do not purify their souls from polytheism through monotheism. This is taken from His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And a soul and He who formed it﴾. Al-Dahhak and Muqatil said: they do not spend in acts of obedience and do not give charity. Mujahid said: they do not purify their deeds (la yuzakkuna a'malahum).

Verily, those who believe and do righteous deeds, theirs is a reward that is not interrupted (ghayr mamnun). That is: it is not bestowed upon them with a reproach (min al-mann), and the root of the word is heaviness; or it is not cut off, from "I cut the rope" (manantu al-habl, qatatuhu).

It was also said: this was revealed concerning the sick and the aged, who when they are unable to perform acts of obedience, have the reward written for them as (equal to) the best of what they used to do.

Say: "Do you indeed disbelieve in Him who created the earth in two days?" This is a rebuke and a severe denunciation of their disbelief. The particle "inna" (indeed) and the lam (emphatic lam) are either for emphasizing the denial, and the placing of the interrogative hamza (the alif of interrogation) at the front is because it requires initial position, not for the sake of emphasizing the denial; or they serve to indicate that their disbelief is so remote that rational people would deny its occurrence, and therefore it requires emphasis. The relative clause is used to attach their disbelief to the words "Him who created the earth in two days," in order to magnify the majesty of Him, exalted is He, and to magnify their disbelief in Him: that is, in the One of great majesty who decreed its existence, meaning He decided that it would come into being within the span of two days, or in two periods, with the understanding that what comes into being in each period comes into being in the swiftest manner possible. Otherwise, the true day only comes into being after its existence, the leveling of the heavens, the origination of their luminaries, and the arrangement of their movements.

"And you set up rivals to Him": this is coordinated with "you disbelieve" and falls under the ruling of denial and reproach. The word "rivals" (andad) is in the plural in view of what actually occurs, not because the basis of the denial is plurality. That is: "and you set up rivals to Him," while the situation is that it is impossible for Him to have even one rival.

"That" (dhalika) is a demonstrative referring to the relative clause, in view of its being characterized by what is in its complement clause, and the sense of distance in it together with the nearness of the reference to what is pointed at, to signal the remoteness of His rank in greatness. The singular form of the second-person pronoun "ka" is used, as has been mentioned many times, since the intent is not to specify the addressees. It is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate (khabar) is what follows: that is, that One of great majesty who did what was mentioned.

"Lord of the worlds": that is, the Creator of all existent things and their Sustainer, not of the earth alone. So how could the lowliest of His creatures be imagined to be a rival to Him?

The utterance of His, exalted is He: ﴿And He placed within it firm mountains﴾ is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) on "خَلَقَ" (khalaqa, "created"), and it falls under the same ruling as the relative clause (ṣila). The "placing" (jaʿl) is creative (ibdāʿī). The objection that a separation (fasl) occurs between the two by two clauses that lie outside the scope of the relative clause is answered: the first of them is connected to His words, ﴿you disbelieve﴾, so it stands in the place of a repetition of it, and the second is a parenthetical clause (jumla iʿtirāḍiyya) that confirms the meaning of the statement, standing in the place of emphasis (taʾkīd). Thus the separation by them is no real separation. In addition, there is the benefit of alerting that the mere coordinated term is sufficient for the establishment of His lordship over the worlds and for the impossibility that a rival be made for Him, so how much more when the coordinated items are joined to it. It has been said that it is a conjunction on an implied term, meaning: He created it, and placed … etc. It has also been said that it is a new independent statement (kalām mustaʾnaf). Whichever is the case, what is meant is the decreeing of the placing, not the placing in actuality.

His, exalted is He, words: ﴿from above it﴾ are connected to "جَعَلَ" (jaʿala, "placed"), or to an implied verb, and it is an attribute (ṣifa) of "رَواسِيَ" (rawāsiya, "firm mountains"), meaning: existing from above it, elevated over it, so that its benefits are made accessible to its inhabitants and what it contains of the sites of reflection (maraṣid al-iʿtibār) and the places where thoughts alight (maṭāriḥ al-afkār) becomes apparent to the observers.

﴿And He blessed in it﴾, meaning: He decreed that its good would increase, by creating the kinds of animals, of which man is one, and the varieties of plants from which their livelihoods come.

﴿And He apportioned in it its sustenance﴾, meaning: He decreed in actuality that there would come into existence, in what will come, for its inhabitants, of the various kinds, their suitable sustenance in a specified measure that wisdom requires. It has been recited "وَقَسَّمَ فِيها أقْواتَها" (wa qassama fīhā aqwātahā, "and He distributed in it its sustenance"). (p-5)﴿in four days﴾ is connected to the occurrence of the mentioned matters, not to their decreeing, meaning: He decreed their occurrence in two days. It was said "in four days" meaning "in complete four," for the explicit statement of the total (faḏlaka).

﴿equally﴾ is a verbal noun (maṣdar) emphasizing an implied term that is an attribute of "أيّامٍ" (ayyām, "days"), meaning: they were equal, equal, i.e., equality, as the reading in the genitive indicates. It has been said that it is a circumstantial state (ḥāl) from the pronoun in "أقْواتِها" or in "فِيها", and it has been recited in the nominative, "سَواءٌ" (sawāʾun), meaning: they are equal.

﴿for those who ask﴾ is connected to an implied term whose estimate is: this restriction is for those who ask about the duration of the creation of the earth and what is in it; or it is connected to "قَدَّرَ" (qaddara, "decreed"), meaning: He decreed in it its sustenance for the sake of those who ask, i.e., those who seek it, who are in need of it, from among those who feed themselves.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 41, verse 11:

The words of the Most High, ﴿Then He turned to the heaven﴾, are the beginning of an explanation of the manner of creation (al-takwin) following the explanation of the manner of measuring out (al-taqdir). Perhaps the restriction of the explanation to what relates to the earth and its inhabitants is because explaining His, exalted is He, care for the addressees and the arrangement of the foundations of their livelihoods before their creation is among the things that move them to faith and restrain them from disbelief and transgression. That is: ﴿then He directed Himself toward it﴾, a upright direction that does not turn aside to anything else.

﴿And it was smoke﴾, i.e., a dark matter by which its substance is expressed, or the minute parts of which it was composed, or smoke rising from the water, as will come later. He specified the turning (al-istiwa') to the heaven, although the address that follows it is directed to both of them together, as His words speak: ﴿So He said to it and to the earth﴾, being content with mention of its measuring out and the measuring out of what is in it, as if it were said: So He said to it and to the earth whose existence was measured out and the existence of what is in it.

﴿Come, both of you﴾, i.e., be, and come into being in a specific manner and at a determined time for each of you. This is an expression for the connection of His will, exalted is He, with their existence, a connection of action, by way of representation, after the decree of their affair, without there being a commander and a commanded, as in His words: ﴿Be﴾. His words, exalted is He, ﴿willingly or unwillingly﴾, are a representation of the inevitability of the effect of His power upon them and the impossibility of their refusing it; they do not establish willingness or unwillingness for them. Both are verbal nouns placed in the position of the circumstantial state, i.e., obedient or unwilling. His words, exalted is He, ﴿They said: We come willingly﴾, i.e., submissive, are a representation of the complete influence upon them, by their very essence, of the Lordly power, and their coming into being as they were commanded, and a depiction that their existence as they are is proceeding in accordance with perfect wisdom, for willingness indicates that, while unwillingness suggests the opposite. "Willingly" was said in view of their being in the position of address and reply, as in His words: ﴿prostrating﴾.

And His saying, ﴿Then He completed them as seven heavens﴾: this is an explanation and elaboration of the summary creation of the heaven, which is expressed by the command (amr) and its response, not that it is an act that follows the creation of the heavens. That is, He created them with an originating creation (khalqan ibda'iyyan) and perfected their matter as wisdom requires. The pronoun refers either to "the heaven" according to its meaning, or it is an undefined pronoun (mubham), and "seven heavens" is a circumstantial accusative (hal) on the first view and a specifying accusative (tamyiz) on the second.

﴿in two days﴾: in a period determined as two days. He has already specified the duration of the creation of the earth and of what is in it when He stated their measure, so the creation of everything occurred in six days, as is stated in various places in the revelation.

﴿And He revealed in each heaven its command﴾: this is coordinated (ma'tuf) with "completed them." That is, He created in each of them what is in the angels, the luminous bodies, and other things that no one knows but God Most High, as Qatadah and al-Suddi said. Thus "revelation" (wahy) is an expression for the act of creation, like "command," restricted by the time that restricts the thing it is coordinated with. Or it means He revealed to the inhabitants of each of them His commands and imposed upon them the obligations that befit them, so it has the same meaning, but it is unrestricted from the mentioned restriction. Whichever it is, according to what has been established of the explanation, there is no indication in the noble verse of an order between the bringing into existence of the earth and the bringing into existence of the heaven. The order is only between the determination (taqdir) and the bringing into existence. As for the case where "creation" and the three verbs coordinated with it are taken in their apparent meanings, then this verse and the verse in Surat al-Baqarah, His saying: ﴿It is He who created for you all that is on the earth; then He turned to the heaven and made them seven heavens﴾, indicate that the creation of the earth and what is in it precedes the creation of the heaven and what is in it. Most of the people of tafsir agree on this.

It has been reported that the Great Throne was upon the water before the creation of the heavens and the earth. Then God Most High caused agitation in the water, so it foamed, and smoke rose from it. The foam remained on the surface of the water, and He created dryness in it and made it one earth, then split it and made it earths. As for the smoke, it rose and ascended, and He created the heavens from it. It has also been reported that He created the body of the earth on Sunday and Monday and spread it out, and created what is in it on Tuesday and Wednesday, and created the heavens and what is in them on Thursday and Friday, and created Adam (peace be upon him) in the last hour of it, which is the hour in which the Hour will be established.

It has been said that the creation of the body of the earth precedes the creation of the heavens, but its spreading out and the creation of what is in it are later than that, due to His saying: ﴿And the earth after that He spread it out﴾. And what is reported from al-Hasan (may God have mercy on him): that God Most High created the earth in the place of Bayt al-Maqdis like a grinding stone (fihr), upon which was smoke clinging to it. Then He raised the smoke and created the heavens from it, held the stone in its place, and spread out the earth from it. This is His saying: ﴿The heavens and the earth were joined together, then We separated them﴾, and so on.

The intended meaning of its being placed together with the heaven in the string of the command to come is not the bringing into existence and origination of the heaven, but the bringing into existence of its spreading out and its being made in a particular manner suitable to it, with a specific shape and a particular attribute. It is as if it were said: Come as you ought to come. Come, O earth, spread out, a resting place and a cradle for your people; and come, O heaven, raised up, a roof for them. The meaning of "coming" is attaining that manner, as is indicated by the reading "ātiyā" and "ātaynā" from al-mu'ātāh, which is agreement. You know that what is mentioned before the command to come is not merely the creation of the body of the earth, so that what was mentioned could be realized; rather, the creation of what is in it, also of matters that come after its spreading out, is certain. So it is more apparent to follow the path of the earlier scholars and to take the command to come as referring to the creation of the two in agreement in the mentioned manner. It is not necessary that its spreading out be an effect of that creation; what is necessary is that the realization of agreement be an effect of it. There is no doubt that the creation of the heaven in the manner appropriate to it is sufficient for its realization, and the creation of the earth in the mentioned manner before that does not undermine this. It is also possible to take "the earth" in His saying ﴿And the earth after that He spread it out﴾ as an object of an implied verb that has been omitted, under the condition of the explanatory (tafsir) structure, and to take "that" as a reference to what was mentioned of the building of the heaven, the raising of its height, its leveling, and other things, not to the heavens themselves. The posteriority may be understood either as meaning that it is inferior to the first in indicating overpowering power, as has been said, or as meaning that it is more binding in obligation, since the benefits attached to what is in the earth are greater, the welfare of people is more closely tied to them, and their knowledge of its details is more complete. What has been reported from al-Hasan (may God be pleased with him) is not an explicit text on the delay of the spreading out of the earth after the creation of the heaven, since the spreading of the earth is coordinated by "and" with the rising of the smoke and the creation of the heaven, so there is no certain indication of order in that. Imam al-Wahidi transmitted from Muqatil that the creation of the heaven precedes the bringing into existence of the earth, let alone its spreading out. So the command to come to both must then also be taken in the mentioned sense of agreement and compliance. The precedence of the creation of the heaven over the creation of the earth does not undermine this, just as the precedence of the creation of the earth over the creation of the heaven did not undermine it. All of this is on the assumption that the word "then" (thumma) indicates temporal sequence. But on the assumption that it indicates sequence of rank (rutbi), as most scholars have inclined, there is no indication in the noble verse of order, as in the first view. On this basis the discussion in the interpretation of His saying ﴿It is He who created for you all that is on the earth﴾ and so on was constructed. The creation there was not taken in the sense of determination, as it was taken here, only so that the position of favor might receive its due.

﴿And We adorned the lowest heaven with lamps﴾: from the stars, for they all appear shining upon it, as if they were in it. The turn to the plural of majesty ("We") is to show greater care for the matter. His saying ﴿and as a protection﴾ is a verbal noun (masdar) emphasizing a verb coordinated with "adorned," that is: and We protected them from calamities, or from the eavesdropping devils, as a protection. It has been said that it is an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu) in meaning, as if it were said: And We created the lamps as an adornment and a protection.

﴿That﴾: what has been mentioned in its details.

﴿is the decree of the Mighty, the All-Knowing﴾: the One who is exceedingly powerful and knowing.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 41, verse 13:

﴿Then if they turn away﴾ is connected to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: Do you indeed...﴾ etc. That is: if they turn away from reflecting upon the great matters mentioned that call to faith, or from faith after this clarification, ﴿then say﴾ to them:

﴿I have warned you﴾, i.e., I warn you. The past form is used to indicate the certainty of the warning, which announces the certainty of what is warned of.

﴿a thunderbolt﴾, i.e., a tremendous punishment of severe impact, as if it were a thunderbolt (ṣāʿiqah).

﴿like the thunderbolt of ʿAd and Thamud﴾. It is also read ṣaʿqatan (a single blast), "like the blast of ʿAd and Thamud." It is the single instance (marrah) of ṣaʿq or ṣaʿaq. It is said: "The thunderbolt struck him with a ṣaʿq, so he was struck down with a ṣaʿq," and it is of the pattern "I did it, so it was done" (faʿaltuhu fafuʿila).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 41, verse 14:

﴿When the messengers came to them﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring back to ﴿the thunderbolt of ʿĀd﴾. There is no soundness in making it a temporal adverb (ẓarf) governed by "I have warned you" (andhartukum), nor an attributive (ṣifa) of "thunderbolt" (ṣāʿiqa), because that corrupts the meaning. As for making it an attribute of "the thunderbolt of ʿĀd", meaning "the one that occurred when they came to them", this involves omitting the relative pronoun together with part of its relative clause.

﴿From before them and from behind them﴾ is connected to "came to them", meaning: from all their sides, and they strove with them from every direction, or from the direction of the past by warning them about what took place among the disbelievers in it, and from the direction of the future by cautioning them about what would befall them of the punishment of this world and the punishment of the Hereafter. It was also said: the meaning is that the messengers, those who came before and those who came after, came to them, treating the coming of their words and their call to the truth as the coming of their persons, for Hud and Salih were both calling them to faith in them and in all the messengers, those who came from before them (i.e., before them) and those who would come from behind them (i.e., after them). It is as though the messengers had come to them and addressed them with His words, exalted is He: ﴿that you should not worship except God﴾, meaning: that you should not worship, where "that" (an) is either a verbal particle (maṣdariyya) or, meaning: do not worship, where it is explanatory (mufassira).

﴿They said: "Had our Lord willed﴾, meaning: (p-8) the sending of messengers, not the sending down of angels as has been said, for that is devoid of conveying what they intended of denying human messengership, and this has passed in what came before.

﴿He would have sent down angels﴾, meaning: He would have sent them, but since their sending would be by way of descent, it is said "would have sent down."

﴿So indeed we disbelieve in that with which you have been sent﴾, meaning: according to your claim, and in this there is a form of mockery of them.

﴿Disbelievers﴾ because you are humans like us, with no superiority for you over us. It is narrated that Abu Jahl said to an assembly of Quraysh: "The matter of Muhammad has become confused for us. If you were to seek for us a man knowledgeable in poetry, soothsaying and magic, so that he might speak with him and then bring us a clarification of his affair." ʿUtba ibn Rabiʿa said: "By God, I have heard poetry, soothsaying and magic, and I have knowledge of that, and nothing of it is hidden from me." So he went to him and said: "O Muhammad, are you better, or Hashim? Are you better, or ʿAbd al-Muttalib? Are you better, or ʿAbd Allah? Why do you revile our gods and mislead us? If you desire leadership, we will make you a leader by raising the banner for you; and if you desire wealth, we will gather for you what will make you rich; and if it is marriage you desire, we will marry you to ten women, choosing whichever daughters of Quraysh you wish." The Messenger of God ﷺ remained silent. When ʿUtba finished, he (ﷺ) said: "In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate, ﴿Ha Mim﴾ up to His words, exalted is He: ﴿like the thunderbolt of ʿĀd and Thamud﴾." So ʿUtba held his hand over his mouth and implored him by the ties of kinship, and he returned to his family and did not go out to Quraysh. When he was delayed from them, they said: "We think ʿUtba has only become a convert (ṣabaʾ)." So they went to him and said: "O ʿUtba, nothing has kept you from us except that you have converted." He became angry and then said: "By God, I spoke to him, and he answered me with something which, by God, is neither poetry, nor soothsaying, nor magic. When he reached ﴿a thunderbolt like the thunderbolt of ʿĀd and Thamud﴾, I held my hand over his mouth and implored him by the ties of kinship that he stop. You know that Muhammad, when he says something, does not lie, so I feared that the punishment would descend upon you."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 41, verse 15:

﴿As for ʿĀd, they were arrogant in the land﴾ This begins the narration of what is specific to each of the two groups in terms of wrongdoing and punishment, following the narration of what applies to all of them in terms of absolute disbelief. That is: they magnified themselves therein over its people, or they rose high therein and gained control over its people.

﴿without right﴾ That is: without any entitlement to self-magnification and dominion.

﴿And they said﴾ relying upon their strength and might.

﴿"Who is mightier than us in strength?"﴾ Since they were tall of body and great in build, and their strength reached the point that a man would pull a rock from a mountain and uproot it with his hand.

﴿Did they not see﴾ That is: were they heedless, or did they not look and did not know with a clear knowledge akin to direct observation and witnessing?

﴿that Allah, who created them, is mightier than them in strength﴾ That is: in power. For He, exalted is He, is Powerful by His essence, has power over what has no end, is strong in what no other can bear, and bestows strength and capacities upon every strong and capable being. He mentioned their creation in the relative clause, rather than the creation of the heavens and the earth, because of their claim to extreme strength; and in this there is a kind of mockery of them.

﴿And they were, of Our signs﴾ those revealed to the messengers.

﴿denying﴾ That is: they rejected them while knowing their reality. This is a conjunction with "they were arrogant" (fa-istakbarū), like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they said﴾; and what lies between them is a parenthetical interjection refuting their vile statement.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 41, verse 16:

﴿So We sent upon them a furious wind﴾ That is: cold, which destroys and burns by the intensity of its coldness, from al-sirr (cold), which is the cold that "yasirr" (gathers and contracts); or violent in its blowing, from al-sarir (roaring).

﴿on days of ill omen﴾ Plural of nahisah, from nahisa, nahsan, the opposite of sa'ida, sa'dan. It is also read with a sukun for lightness, or as an adjective in the form fa'l, or as a description by a verbal noun for emphasis. It has been said: they were from the last Wednesday of Shawwal to the next Wednesday, and no people were punished except on a Wednesday.

﴿That We might make them taste the torment of disgrace in the life of this world﴾ It is also read "litudhiqahum" (that He might make them taste), with the act of making taste attributed to the wind or to the days. The torment is attributed to disgrace, which is humiliation and abasement, on the basis that it is a description of it, as indicated by His saying, ﴿And the torment of the Hereafter is more disgracing﴾. In reality, disgrace is a description of the one tormented, but it has been applied to the torment for emphasis.

﴿And they will not be helped﴾ by averting the torment from them in any way.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 41, verse 17:

﴿And as for Thamud, We guided them﴾ — We showed them the truth by setting up the created signs (al-ayat al-takwiniyyah), by sending the messengers, and by sending down the legislative signs (al-ayat al-tashri'iyyah), and We completely removed their excuses. The realisation of the meaning of guidance (al-huda) has already been discussed in the commentary on His, exalted is He, words: ﴿a guidance for those who are mindful of God﴾. It is also read "Thamud" in the accusative, governed by a verb that is explained by what follows it, and read with tanwin in both cases, and with a dammah on the tha'.

﴿So they preferred blindness over guidance﴾ — that is, they chose misguidance over guidance.

﴿So the bolt of the humiliating punishment seized them﴾ — the calamity of punishment and the striking disaster of punishment. Al-hawn means humiliation; the punishment is described by it for emphasis, or it is put in apposition to it (badal).

﴿for what they had been earning﴾ — namely, from their choosing misguidance.
And We saved those who had believed and used to be mindful of God (﴿وَنَجَّيْنا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا وكانُوا يَتَّقُونَ﴾) from that thunderbolt.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 41, verse 19:

﴿And on the Day when the enemies of Allah are gathered﴾ This begins the explanation of their deferred punishments, following the explanation of their immediate punishments. Referring to them as "the enemies of Allah" serves to censure them and to signal the reason for the various kinds of torment that befall them. It has been said: the intended meaning is the disbelievers of the earlier and later generations, but this is refuted by His statement that follows: ﴿among nations that passed away before them, of jinn and humankind﴾. It is also read as "yaḥshuru" (with the verb in the active voice and "a'dā'a Allāh" in the accusative), and with the nun of majesty (nūn al-'azama), with the shin either vowelled with a ḍamma or with a kasra.

﴿to the Fire﴾ That is, to the place of reckoning, for there the testimony that follows will be realized, not by the incompleteness of question and answer. Their being driven to the Fire, and the expression of it as "the Fire," is either to signal that it is the consequence of their gathering, on the verge of entering it, or because their reckoning will take place at its edge. "The Day" (yawma) is either in the accusative governed by "remember" (udhkur), or it is an adverbial complement of a deferred implied verb that has been omitted, to create an impression of the inadequacy of expression to detail it, as has passed in His statement: ﴿the Day when Allah gathers the Messengers﴾. It has been said: it is an adverbial complement of what His statement ﴿so they will be held back﴾ indicates, meaning: the first of them will be held back until the last of them, so that they catch up with one another; and this is an expression of their great number. It has also been said: they will be driven and pushed into the Fire.

And His saying, ﴿until, when they arrive at it﴾, meaning all of them together, is the endpoint for [the gathering] "they are gathered" (yuhsharu) or "they are held back in ranks" (yuwza'un). That is, [it means] until, when they are present there. The particle "ma" (ما) is an extra particle (ma zaa'idah, a superfluous particle inserted for emphasis), used to stress the close connection between the testimony and their presence.

﴿Their hearing, their sight, and their skins will testify against them concerning what they used to do﴾ in the worldly life, of the various kinds of disbelief and disobedience, by Allah the Exalted making them speak, or by displaying upon them the traces of what they committed through them. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the intended meaning of the testimony of the skins is the testimony of the private parts (furuj), and this is the more fitting [interpretation], given that the question is specified with them in His saying, Exalted is He:

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 41, verse 21:**

﴿And they will say to their skins, "Why did you testify against us?"﴾ For what the skins testify to, namely fornication (*zina*, unlawful sexual intercourse), is a greater crime and ugliness, and more conducive to disgrace and punishment, than what the hearing and the sight testify to of the sins committed through them. It is also said: what is meant by "skins" is the limbs (*jawarih*, the bodily organs). That is, they asked them as a rebuke, as it is reported that they said to them: "It was on your behalf that we were contending," and in another narration: "Away with you, and destruction! On your behalf I was disputing." The use of the plural form for rational beings in addressing the skins, and in His saying, ﴿They will say: "Allah has made us speak, He who made everything speak."﴾, is because they are in the position of question and answer, which is specific to rational beings. That is: "Allah, who made everything speak, made us speak and enabled us to state the truth, so we testified against you concerning the ugly deeds you committed through us, and we did not conceal them." It is also said: "We did not speak by our own choice; rather, Allah, who makes everything speak, made us speak." But this is not the correct reading, because it gives the impression of compulsion in the reporting. It is also said: they asked them as an expression of amazement, and the meaning then is: "Our speech is not something strange from the power of Allah, who makes every living thing speak."

﴿And He it is who created you the first time, and to Him you will be returned.﴾ For whoever is able to create you and bring you into being at first, and to restore you and return you to His recompense a second time, is not to be marvelled at for making your limbs speak. Perhaps the use of the present tense (*turja'un*, "you are returned") is employed even though this dialogue takes place after resurrection and return, because the meaning of "return" is not merely being restored to life through resurrection, but includes everything that encompasses it and follows from it, namely everlasting punishment. This is realized in the dialogue by treating what is expected as if it were actual. Moreover, it observes the rhyme of the verse endings (*fawasil*, the rhyming pauses of the verses).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 41, verse 22:

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And you did not used to conceal yourselves lest your hearing and your sight and your skins should testify against you﴾. It is a report of what will be said to them on that Day, from Him, exalted is He, by way of reproach and rebuke, confirming the answer of the skins; that is: you did not used to conceal yourselves in the world when committing the abominations, out of fear that your limbs would testify against you concerning that, as you used to conceal yourselves from the people out of fear of being exposed before them. Rather, you were denying the Resurrection and the Recompense altogether.

﴿But you thought that Allah does not know much of what you do﴾ of the hidden ugly deeds, so He will not expose them in the Hereafter; and for this reason you became bold in what you did. In this there is an indication that the testimony of the limbs is by His, exalted is He, informing then, not that they were aware of what they testified to at the moment it proceeded from them. From Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: I was concealed behind the curtains of the Ka'bah, when three men entered: two from Thaqif and one from Quraysh, or two from Quraysh and one from Thaqif. One of them said: Do you think that Allah hears what we say? The other said: He hears if we speak aloud, and does not hear if we conceal it. So I mentioned that to the Prophet ﷺ, and Allah, exalted is He, revealed: ﴿And you did not used to conceal yourselves﴾, the verse. Accordingly, the ruling reported then would be specific to those among the disbelievers who held that belief. Perhaps the more fitting view is that by "thought" (al-zann) is meant a figurative meaning that encompasses its literal meaning and what runs in its course of actions that indicate it, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He thinks that his wealth will make him immortal﴾, so that what is reported of the state encompasses all categories of the disbelievers. So reflect.

That is, (ذَلِكُمْ) is a demonstrative pointing to what was mentioned of your assumption, and the sense of distance in it is to indicate the extreme remoteness of their rank in evil and wickedness. It is the subject (mubtada'), and the words of the Exalted: ﴿ظَنُّكُمُ الَّذِي ظَنَنْتُمْ بِرَبِّكُمْ أَرْدَاكُمْ﴾ ("That your assumption which you assumed about your Lord has destroyed you") are two predicates (khabarān) for it. It is also permissible for "ظَنُّكُمْ" (zannukum, your assumption) to be a substitute (badal) and "أَرْدَاكُمْ" (ardākum, has destroyed you) the predicate.

﴿فَأَصْبَحْتُمْ﴾ (fa-asbahtum, so you became) by reason of that evil assumption which destroyed you.

﴿مِنَ الْخَاسِرِينَ﴾ (mina al-khasirin, among the losers), since what they had been given for attaining the happiness of both abodes became a cause of misery in both lives.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 41, verse 24:

﴿Whether they endure patiently, the Fire is their abode.﴾ That is, it is a place of dwelling and everlasting residence for them, such that there is no escape for them from it. The shift to the third person (ghayba) is to signal that their condition calls for them to be turned away from and their bad state to be related to others, or to indicate that they are removed from the sphere of address and cast into the deepest levels (darakat) of the Fire.

﴿And if they seek to be pleased (yasta'tibu),﴾ that is, they ask for al-'utba, which is returning to what they love, out of distress at what they are in.

﴿then they are not among those who are granted it (al-mu'tabin).﴾ That is, those who are answered in it. A parallel to this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It is all the same for us whether we rage or endure patiently; there is no escape for us.﴾ It has also been read as "wa-in yasta'tibu fa-ma hum mina al-mu'tibin," meaning: if they ask to make their Lord content, they are not doing it, because the capacity has passed.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 41, verse 25:

﴿And We appointed for them companions﴾: that is, We predestined and paired them with the disbelievers in this world.

﴿Companions (qurana')﴾: plural of qarin (companion), that is, close friends (akhdan) from among the devils, who take control over them with the control of the qayd (the shell-covering) over the bayd (the egg), and the qayd is the shell. It is also said that the origin of qayd is exchange (badal), and from it comes muqayada (barter), meaning mutual exchange.

﴿So they made attractive to them what was before them﴾: of the affairs of this world and the pursuit of desires.

﴿And what was behind them﴾: of the affairs of the Hereafter, since they showed them that there is no resurrection, no reckoning, and nothing disagreeable at all.

﴿And the word has been justified against them﴾: that is, the word of punishment was established and confirmed against them, and its requirement and its fulfilment came to pass. This is His, exalted is He, saying to Iblis: ﴿Then the truth is, and the truth I say: I will surely fill Hell with you and with those among them who follow you, all together﴾ [38:84–85]. And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Whoever follows you among them, I will surely fill Hell with you all together﴾ [7:18], as has passed many times.

﴿Among nations﴾: a circumstantial phrase (hal) from the pronoun in the genitive case (al-damir al-majrur), that is, existing within the totality of nations. It is also said that "fi" here means "ma'a" (with). As you see, this is clearly indicating that what is meant by the enemies of God Most High in what preceded is the known ones from 'Ad and Thamud, not the disbelievers of the earlier and later generations, as has been said.

﴿That had passed away﴾: an attribute of umam (nations), that is, they had gone by.

﴿Before them, of jinn and humankind﴾: upon disbelief and disobedience, like the custom of these people.

﴿Indeed they were losers﴾: a causal clause explaining their deserving of punishment, and the harm (al-dayr) applies to the earlier and later ones alike.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 41, verse 26:

﴿And those who disbelieved said﴾, from among the leaders of the polytheists, to their followers, or some of them said to others:

﴿Do not listen to this Qur'an﴾, that is: do not pay attention to it (lit. do not be silent to listen to it).

﴿And make noise during it﴾, and oppose it with nonsense, such as rajaz (rhythmic verse) and poetry, and whistling (tasdiyah) and clapping (muka'), or raise your voices with them so that you confuse it for the reciter. It is also read with a damma on the ghayn (*yalghu*), and the meaning is one: it is said *laghā yalghā* like *laqiya yalqā*, and *laghā yalghū* when one talks nonsense (*hadhā*).

﴿So that you may prevail﴾, that is: that you may overcome it (i.e. the recitation of it).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 41, verse 27:

﴿So We will surely make those who disbelieve taste a severe punishment﴾: that is, by Allah, We will surely make these sayers and those who engage in idle talk taste it, or all the disbelievers, and they are included among them by primary inclusion (dukhulan awwaliyyan).

﴿a severe punishment﴾: whose extent cannot be measured.

﴿And We will surely recompense them with the worst of what they used to do﴾: that is, the recompense for the evil deeds of their actions, which are in themselves the worst. It has been said that He does not recompense them for their good deeds, such as aiding the distressed, maintaining ties of kinship, and hospitality to guests, because these are nullified by disbelief. And it is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father: "a severe punishment" refers to the Day of Badr, and "the worst of what they used to do" refers to what they did in the Hereafter.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 41, verse 28:

﴿Dhalika﴾ is the subject (mubtada') and His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿the requital of the enemies of Allah﴾ is its predicate (khabar). That is: what has been mentioned of requital is a requital prepared for His enemies, Exalted is He. His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿the Fire﴾ is an explicative apposition (‘atf bayan) to "the requital." Or "dhalika" is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: the matter is that, [the demonstrative] being an expression for the content of the sentence and not for the requital. And what follows it is an independent sentence explaining what precedes it. His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿For them therein is the abode of eternity﴾ is an independent sentence confirming what precedes it. Or "the Fire" is the subject (mubtada') and "hiya" (it) is its predicate, meaning: it itself is their abode of residence. The "fi" (in) here is for abstraction (al-tajrid), which is extracting from a thing possessing a quality another thing like it, as hyperbole for its perfection in that quality, as one says: "In the egg are twenty ratls of iron." It has also been said: [the "fi"] retains its own meaning, and the intended sense is that for them, in the Fire which contains the degrees, there is a specific abode in which they abide forever.

﴿A requital for what they used to deny of Our signs﴾ is in the accusative, governed by an omitted verb, meaning: they are requited with a requital; or by the preceding verbal noun (masdar), since a masdar is put in the accusative by one like it, as in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, Hell is your requital, a full requital﴾. The first "ba'" (for/because of) is connected to "jaza'an" (requital), and the second to "yajhadun" (they deny), which has been placed before it for the sake of observing the rhyme (fawasil). That is: because of what they used to deny Our true signs, or used to engage in idle talk concerning them. He mentioned denial because it is the cause of idle talk.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 41, verse 29:

﴿And those who disbelieved said﴾ — while they are being turned over in what was mentioned of the punishment.

﴿Our Lord, show us those two who led us astray from among the jinn and mankind﴾ — they mean the two groups of devils of both kinds (jinn and men), who were assigned to them as companions (muqayyadan), who carry them to disbelief and sins through enticement (taswil) and adornment (tazyin). It has been said: they are Iblis and Qabil, for they established disbelief and killing without right. It was also read as "arna" (with the vowel of the ra' lightened), like "fakhdh" for "fakhidh." It has also been said that its meaning is: give us them (a'tina huma). It was also read with the short vowel of the ra' being dropped (ikhtilas kasrat al-ra').

﴿That we may place them beneath our feet﴾ — that is, we trample them in vengeance upon them. It has been said: we place them in the lowest level of the Fire (al-darak al-asfal).

﴿So that they may be among the lowest﴾ — that is, in humiliation and disgrace, or in position (makanan).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 41, verse 30:

﴿Indeed, those who said, "Our Lord is Allah"﴾ This begins the explanation of the good state of the believers in this world and the Hereafter, after the explanation of the evil state of the disbelievers in both. That is: they said, acknowledging His lordship, may He be exalted, and affirming His oneness.

﴿Then they remained steadfast﴾ That is: they held firm to the affirmation and what it requires. "Then" (thumma) here indicates sequence either in time or in rank, for steadfastness carries the whole matter. What is related from the Rightly Guided Caliphs, may Allah be pleased with them, regarding its meaning, namely firmness in faith, sincerity in deeds, and performance of the obligations, is an explanation of its particulars.

﴿The angels descend upon them﴾ from Him, may He be exalted; they assist them in the religious and worldly matters that occur to them, with what expands their breasts and removes from them fear and sorrow, by way of inspiration, just as the disbelievers are led astray by the evil companions assigned to them, through the adornment of ugly deeds. It was said: they descend at death with glad tidings. It was said: when they rise from their graves. It was said: the glad tidings are in three places: at death, in the grave, and at resurrection. The most evident view is generality and absoluteness, as you will come to know.

﴿"Do not fear"﴾ what you are about to face, for fear is a distress that befalls a person in anticipation of something disliked.

﴿"And do not grieve"﴾ over what you have left behind, for grief is a distress that befalls a person upon the occurrence of the loss of something beneficial or the attainment of something harmful. It was said: the intended meaning is a prohibition against distresses in general, and the meaning is: Allah, may He be exalted, has decreed for you safety from every distress, so you will never taste it. "An" (that) is either explanatory (mufassirah) or the lightened form (mukhaffafah) of the heavy form, and the original is "annahu la takhafu," with the hā' being the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-sha'n). It was read "lā takhāfū," meaning: they say, "Do not fear," and it is either a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the angels or a resumptive new sentence (isti'nāf).

﴿"And rejoice"﴾ That is: be glad.

﴿"In the Garden which you were promised"﴾ in the world through the tongues of the messengers. This is among their glad tidings in one of the three places.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 41, verse 31:

And His saying, the Exalted: ﴿We are your allies in the life of this world﴾ ...etc. Among their glad tidings in this world, that is: We are your helpers in your affairs, We inspire you with the truth and guide you to what is good for you and your welfare. And perhaps this is an expression of what occurs to the minds of believers who persist in acts of obedience, that this is by God the Exalted's granting of success and His support for them through the intermediary of the angels, peace be upon them.

﴿And in the Hereafter﴾ We will supply you with intercession and receive you with honour, when there occurs between the disbelievers and their companions what occurs of enmity and dispute.

﴿And for you therein﴾ that is: in the Hereafter.

﴿Whatever your souls desire﴾ of the various kinds of good things.

﴿And for you therein is whatever you call for﴾ whatever you wish for. Ta-da'una is an iftial form from the du'a' (supplication) in the sense of request, that is: you call for yourselves. It is more general than the first. And "lakum" in both places is a predicate, and "ma" is the subject, and "fīhā" is a circumstantial clause from its pronoun in the predicate. Not confining the second to coordination with "ma tashtahī" is for fullness in the glad tidings and to indicate the independence of each of them.

﴿An entertainment from the Most Forgiving, the Most Merciful﴾. It is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) qualifying what they ask for (mā tadda'ūn), indicating that what they wish for, in relation to the great rewards they are given, is like the nuzul (the provision of hospitality prepared for a guest) given to a guest.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 41, verse 33:

﴿And who is better in speech than one who calls to Allah﴾ That is: to His Oneness, exalted is He, and to obedience to Him. On the authority of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: it is the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) who called to Islam (p-14) and, from him, that they are the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). It has been said: it was revealed concerning the muezzins (mu'adhdhinun). The truth is that its ruling is general for everyone who combines the praiseworthy qualities mentioned in it, even though it was revealed concerning those who were mentioned.

﴿and does righteous deeds﴾ in what is between him and his Lord.

﴿and says: Indeed I am of the Muslims﴾ either out of joy at being one of them, or by taking Islam as a religion and creed. From their saying "this is the saying of so-and-so," meaning his school of thought, not that he literally spoke these words. It was also read as "innī" with a single nun.

Abu al-Su'ud, *Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim*, on surah 41, verse 34:

﴿Nor are the good deed and the evil deed equal.﴾ This is a *jumla mustaʾnafa* (a resumptive sentence, grammatically independent of what precedes it). It is brought to explain the excellent deeds that take place among servants, following the explanation of the excellent deeds that take place between the servant and the Lord, Mighty and Majestic. It serves as an encouragement to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) to be patient with the harm of the polytheists and to repay their evil with good. That is: the good trait and the evil trait are not equal in their effects and rulings. The second *lā* (لا) is *zāʾida* (superfluous, added for emphasis) to reinforce the negation.

As for His words, exalted is He: ﴿Repel [evil] with that which is better⁠﴾ ... etc., this is a resumptive sentence explaining the good outcome of the good deed. That is: repel the evil when an enemy of yours confronts you with the best of the good deeds by which it can be repelled, such as doing good to one who has wronged you, for this is better than pardon. It is placed in the form of an answer to the question of one who asks, "How should I act?" for emphasis. For this reason, he placed *aḥsan* (أحسن) in the position of *al-ḥasana* (الحسنة).

His words, exalted is He: ﴿Then, behold, the one between whom and you there is enmity [will become] as though he were a devoted friend⁠﴾ are an explanation of the result of the repelling that was commanded. That is: when you do this, your hostile opponent becomes like a sincere, compassionate friend.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 41, verse 35:

﴿وَما يُلَقّاها﴾ That is: none receives this quality and disposition (al-khisla wa'l-sajiyya), which is repaying evil with good.

﴿إلا الَّذِينَ صَبَرُوا﴾ That is: patience is their characteristic (sha'nuhum al-sabr).

﴿وَما يُلَقّاها إلا ذُو حَظٍّ عَظِيمٍ﴾ Possessor of a great portion (dhu hazz 'azim) of goodness and perfection of the soul. It is said: the great portion is Paradise. It is said: it is the reward. It is said: it was revealed concerning Abu Sufyan ibn Harb, who used to harm the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and then became a sincere friend (waliyyan musafiyyan).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 41, verse 36:

﴿And if an evil suggestion comes to you﴾ from Satan.

﴿Nazgh﴾ (a prick, an incitement): al-nazgh and al-nasgh have the same meaning, and it is a kind of pricking (nakhs). The whispering of Satan was likened to it, because it is a urging towards evil. [Satan] is described as one who pricks (nazigh) following the pattern of "jadd jadduhu" (its root is the same as its intensive form), or the intended meaning is: "and if a pricker pricks you," with "nazigh" being a verbal description of Satan through the verbal noun. That is: and if Satan diverts you from what you were enjoined to do, namely repelling [evil] with that which is better.

﴿So seek refuge in Allah﴾ from his evil, and do not cut it off.

﴿Indeed, He is the All-Hearing﴾ of your seeking refuge.

﴿the All-Knowing﴾ of your intention, or of your righteousness. And in making the abandonment of repelling with what is better one of the effects of the pricks of Satan, there is an added warning and a repelling of him.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 41, verse 37:

﴿And among His signs﴾ that point to His great affairs.

﴿The night and the day, and the sun and the moon﴾ Each of them is a created being among His creations, subjected to His command.

﴿Do not prostrate to the sun or to the moon﴾ because they are among His created beings, subjected to His commands just like you.

﴿But prostrate to God, who created them﴾ The pronoun refers to the four, because the rule for a group of non-rational beings is the rule of the feminine singular or the feminine plural. Or because it refers to the signs. The linking of the verb to all of them, although the statement that the sun and moon are created is sufficient, serves to indicate the complete removal of these two from the rank of being worthy of worship, by placing them in the category of created things within the class of accidents, which have no independent subsistence. This is the secret of arranging all of them in the series of His signs, may He be exalted: ﴿If it is Him that you worship﴾, for prostration is the highest degree of worship, so it must be restricted to Him, glorified is He. This is a place of prostration according to al-Shafi'i, may God have mercy on him, and according to us it is at the end of the other verse, because it completes the meaning.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 41, verse 38:

﴿Then if they are arrogant﴾ against complying (al-imtithal).

﴿Then those who are with your Lord﴾ from among the angels.

﴿glorify Him night and day﴾ i.e., constantly.

﴿and they never tire﴾ they do not slacken, nor do they grow weary. It was also read "lā yi'samūn" with a kasra on the ya'.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 41, verse 39:

﴿And among His signs is that you see the earth humbled﴾ dry and flattened; it is a metaphor borrowed from khushu' (humility), in the sense of submission.

﴿Then when We send down water upon it﴾ that is, rain.

﴿it stirs and swells﴾ that is, it moves with plant growth and swells, because when the plant is about to emerge, the earth rises up for it and swells, then it splits open for the plant. It was also said: it adorns itself with plants. And it was read as "raba'at" (rabat), that is, it rose up.

﴿Indeed, He who revived it﴾ by what has been mentioned, after its death.

﴿is certainly the Reviver of the dead﴾ by resurrection.

﴿And He is over all things Competent﴾ among the things of which reviving is part.

﴿Competent﴾ exaggerating in power (qadir, a form denoting intensity).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 41, verse 40:

﴿Indeed, those who deviate (yulhidūn)﴾ incline away from uprightness (al-istiqāmah). It is also read as "yalhidūn."

﴿concerning Our signs﴾ by slandering them and distorting them, by interpreting them according to false meanings.

﴿are not hidden from Us﴾ so We will requite them for their deviation. His words, exalted is He: ﴿Is he who is thrown into the Fire better, or he who comes secure on the Day of Resurrection?﴾ are a reminder of the manner of the recompense.

﴿Do whatever you will﴾ of the deeds that lead to what has been mentioned, namely being thrown into the Fire and coming secure. In it is a severe threat.

﴿Indeed, He is Seeing of what you do﴾ so He will recompense you according to your deeds.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 41, verse 41:

And His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in the Reminder when it comes to them﴾ is a substitute (badal) for His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿Indeed, those who distort [the signs]﴾ ... and so on. The predicate of inna (inna's khabar) is the predicate mentioned earlier. It has been said: it is a new, resumed sentence (mustaʼnaf) and its predicate is omitted. Al-Kisa'i said: the earlier predicate has taken its place. And al-Dhikr (the Reminder) means: the Qur'an. And His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿And indeed it is a Book of might﴾ means: abundant in benefits, unparalleled, or invulnerable, such that no one can attempt to produce its like. It is a circumstantial clause (jumlah haliyyah) conveying the extent of the heinousness (shana'a) of disbelieving in it. (p-16)

The commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 41, verse 42:

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Falsehood cannot approach it from before it or from behind it﴾, meaning: falsehood cannot reach it from any of the directions, being a second attribute of "a Book" (kitab). And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿A revelation from One who is All-Wise, Praiseworthy﴾ is either the predicate of an omitted subject (mubtada'), or a further attribute of "a Book" conveying its grandeur through what is added to it (al-fakhamah al-idafiyyah), just as the two preceding attributes convey its grandeur in its essence (al-fakhamah al-dhatiyyah). And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿It cannot approach it﴾ ... etc. is a parenthetical clause (i'tirad) according to those who do not permit placing a non-explicit attribute before an explicit one. All of this is for emphasizing the invalidity of disbelief in the Qur'an.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 41, verse 43:

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿What is said to you﴾ ... etc. is a consolation to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for what he suffers from the harm of the disbelievers. That is: what is said concerning you and concerning what has been sent down to you of the Qur'an, from the side of the disbelievers of your people.

﴿Nothing is said to you except what was said to the messengers before you﴾. That is: nothing but the like of what was said concerning them, of that which contains no good.

﴿Indeed, your Lord is Possessor of forgiveness﴾ for His prophets.

﴿And Possessor of painful punishment﴾ for their enemies. He has already given victory to the messengers before you and taken vengeance upon their enemies, and He will do the like for you as well, and against your enemies.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 41, verse 44:

﴿And if We had made it a non-Arabic Qur'an﴾ is the answer to their saying: "Why was the Qur'an not sent down in the language of non-Arabs?" The pronoun refers to the Reminder (al-dhikr).

﴿They would have said: "Why have its verses not been made clear?"﴾ That is: explained in a tongue we understand. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿What, a non-Arabic (speech) and an Arab (messenger)?﴾ is a denial that establishes the restriction. The word a'jami (non-Arabic) is applied to speech that is not understood and to the one who speaks it, and the yā' (in a'jamī) is for intensification in the description, like aḥmarī (very red). The meaning is: is it a non-Arabic speech while the messenger, or the one addressed by it, is Arab? The singular is used even though those addressed are a great nation, because the intent is to show the incompatibility and discordance between the speech and the one it is addressed to, not to show whether the addressee is one or many. It is also read as a'jamiyyun, meaning: a speech attributed to the nation of non-Arabs. It is read as a'jamiyyun in the form of a report that the Qur'an is non-Arabic while the speaker and the addressee are Arab. It is also permissible that the intent is: "Why were its verses not made clear," so that some of them are non-Arabic to make non-Arabs understand and some Arabic to make Arabs understand. Whichever of these is the case, the purpose is to show that whatever form God's signs came to them in, they found in them a pretext for obstinacy, by which they make excuses.

﴿Say: It is, for those who believe, a guidance﴾ leading them to the truth.

﴿and a healing﴾ for what is in the breasts of doubt and dubiety.

﴿And those who do not believe﴾ is the subject (mubtada'), whose predicate is ﴿in their ears is a deafness﴾, on the reckoning that the sense is: "it," i.e., the Qur'an, is in their ears a deafness, with "deafness" (waqr) being the predicate of the implied pronoun, and "in their ears" being related to an omitted element that occurs as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) of "waqr." This is more fitting with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and it is blindness for them﴾. It has also been said: the predicate of the relative clause is "in their ears," and "waqr" is the subject of the adverbial phrase. It has also been said: "waqr" is the subject, the adverbial phrase is its predicate, and the whole clause is the predicate of the relative clause. It has also been said that the reckoning is: "And those who do not believe, in their ears there is deafness from it." Whoever permits conjunction over two governing elements conjoins the relative clause to the first relative clause, meaning: it is a guidance and a healing for the former, and for the latter a deafness in their ears.

﴿Those﴾ is a reference to the second relative clause, in view of its being characterized by what is within its relative sphere, and considering what is affirmed of them, and the sense of distance in it together with the nearness of the reference to what is pointed at, to indicate the remoteness of their rank in evil, along with what it has of complete suitability to the call from a distance. That is: those remote ones, described by what has been mentioned of being deaf to the truth that they hear and blind to the manifest signs that they see.

﴿They are called from a distant place﴾ is a parable for them in their not accepting and not listening to it, by one who is called from a far distance from which voices can hardly be heard.

And We certainly gave Moses the Book, but it was disputed about. (A new statement, brought to explain that disagreement over scriptures is an old custom among nations and not specific to your people, following the method of His words: ﴿Nothing is said to you except what was said to the messengers before you﴾.) That is: and by Allah, We certainly gave him the Torah, and it was disputed about, so some affirmed it and some denied it. Likewise is the condition of your people regarding what We have given you of the Qur'an: some believe in it and some disbelieve.

﴿And were it not for a word that had preceded from your Lord﴾ concerning your denying nation, namely the promise to delay their punishment and to settle the disputes between them and the believers until the Day of Resurrection, in the manner of His words: ﴿Rather, the Hour is their appointed time﴾ and His words: ﴿But He defers them until an appointed term﴾.

﴿the matter would have been decided between them﴾ by the annihilation of the deniers, as He did with the deniers of earlier nations.

﴿And indeed they﴾ — that is, the disbelievers of your people —

﴿are in disquieting doubt concerning it﴾ — that is, concerning the Qur'an. Making the first pronoun refer to the Jews and the second to the Torah is without any justification.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 41, verse 46:

﴿Whoever does righteousness﴾ by believing in the Books and acting in accordance with what they require.

﴿then it is for his own self﴾; that is, ﴿for his own self﴾ he does it, or its benefit returns to his own self and not to anyone else.

﴿And whoever does evil, it is against it﴾; its harm falls upon him and not upon anyone else.

﴿And your Lord is not ever unjust to the servants﴾ is a concluding parenthetical clause (i'tirad tadhyili) confirming the content of what precedes it. It is built upon treating the withholding of reward from the one who does good for his deed, or the granting of reward to another for his deed, and the punishment of one without wrongdoing or for the wrongdoing of another, as if it were injustice (zulm), which is impossible for Him, glory be to Him and exalted. The detailed verification (tahqiq wa tafsil) of this matter has already passed in Surat Al 'Imran and Surat al-Anfal.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 41, verse 47:

﴿To Him is referred the knowledge of the Hour.﴾ That is: if he is asked about it, it is said, "Allah knows," or, "None knows it except Allah, the Exalted."

﴿And no fruit comes out of its sheaths (akmam).﴾ That is, out of their containers (awiya), the plural of kimm (كِمٍّ), with a kasra, which is the covering of the fruit, like the sheath (juff) of the spathe (talʿa). It has been read as "min thamara" (مِن ثَمَرَةٍ) in the singular, intending the genus (jins), and the plural is used because of the difference in kinds. It has also been read with the pronoun in the plural. "Ma" is negating, and the first "min" is extra (mazida), for the sake of comprehensiveness (istighraq). The possibility that "ma" is relative (mawsula), conjoined to "al-sa'a," with "min" being explanatory (mubayyina), is far-fetched.

﴿And no female conceives or gives birth.﴾ That is, her burden (hamlaha). His saying, ﴿except with His knowledge﴾, is an exceptive clause (istithna' mufarragh, an exception with no stated first part, the exception here being from the most general of states), meaning: nothing happens of the emergence of a fruit, nor the conceiving of a pregnant woman, nor the giving birth of one who gives birth, except that it occurs accompanied by His all-encompassing knowledge, in accompaniment with some of the things.

﴿And on the day He calls to them, "Where are My partners?"﴾ That is, according to your claim, as stated in His saying: ﴿Call upon those partners of Mine whom you claimed.﴾ In it is mockery of them and rebuke to them. "Yawm" (day) is governed by "udhkur" (remember), or it is an adverbial of an implied verb placed later, which has been omitted to signal that explanation falls short of it, as in His saying: ﴿the day Allah gathers the Messengers.﴾

﴿They will say, "We have informed You."﴾ That is, "We have told You."

﴿None of us is a witness.﴾ That is, none of us bears witness to them that they are partners, since we have disowned them when we witnessed the situation. Or: none of us is a person who is a witness; none of us is monotheist for You. Or: none of us can see them, because they have strayed from them at that time. It has been said: this is the speech of the partners, meaning: none of us is a witness who testifies for them that they were righteous. Their saying "We have informed You" is either because this rebuke is preceded by another rebuke, answered with this answer, or because its meaning is: "You now know from our hearts and beliefs that we do not bear that false testimony," since when He knows it from their souls, it is as though they had informed Him of it; or because its meaning is the performative (inshaʾ) rather than the informative (ikhbar), with a notification that existed before that.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 41, verse 48:

﴿And those they used to call upon will have vanished from them﴾, i.e., they used to worship.

﴿Before﴾, i.e., they became absent from them, or the uselessness of them became evident, so their presence was like their absence.

﴿And they will be certain﴾, i.e., they will have certainty.

﴿That they have no escape﴾, i.e., no refuge (mahrab). The verb of thinking (zann) here is suspended from its object by the negative particle.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 41, verse 49:

﴿Man does not tire of asking for good﴾ i.e., he does not grow weary or slacken.

﴿of asking for good﴾: that is, of seeking abundance in blessing and the means of livelihood. It is also read as "min du'a'i bil-khayr" (of asking with good).

﴿But when evil touches him﴾ i.e., hardship and distress.

﴿Then he is despairing, utterly hopeless﴾: here there is intensification in terms of the form (al-bina', the pattern of the word), in terms of repetition, and in terms of the fact that qunut (qunut, "despair") is an expression for excessive hopelessness whose effect appears on the person, so that he shrinks and is broken. That is, he is exaggerated in cutting off hope in the grace and mercy of Allah the Exalted. This is a description of the category by the attribute of most of its individuals, because hopelessness of the mercy of Allah the Exalted can only come from the disbeliever, and He will state this explicitly.

﴿And if We let him taste mercy from Us after adversity had touched him﴾, by relieving him of it.

﴿He will surely say, "This is mine"﴾, meaning: it is my due, which I deserve because of the merit and works I have; or it is mine and not for anyone else, so it will never leave me forever.

﴿And I do not think the Hour will be established﴾, meaning: it will come into being in what is to come.

﴿And if I am returned to my Lord﴾, on the assumption that it is established.

﴿Indeed, with Him I shall have the best﴾, meaning: the best state of honor. This is because he believes that what befell him of worldly blessings was due to his deserving it, and that the blessings of the Hereafter are likewise.

﴿Then We will surely inform those who disbelieved of what they did﴾, meaning: We will make them know the reality of their deeds when We display them in the form of their reality. Its verification has already passed in Surah al-A'raf, at His saying: ﴿And the weighing that Day is the truth﴾, and in His saying: ﴿Your rebellion is only against yourselves﴾ in Surah Yunus.

﴿And We will surely make them taste a severe punishment﴾, whose measure cannot be gauged and whose reality cannot be reached.

(p-19)﴿And when We bestow favor upon man, he turns away and withdraws to one side; and when harm touches him, he is one of lengthy supplication﴾.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 41, verse 51:

﴿And when We bestow favor upon man, he turns away﴾, i.e., from gratitude.

﴿and turns aside with his side﴾, i.e., he goes off by himself and distances himself entirely, out of arrogance and self-magnification. The "side" (al-janib) is a metaphor for the self, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿in regard to what I neglected of Allah﴾. It is also permissible that it means his flank (ʿitf), and it is an expression for deviation and turning away, as they say: "he turned his flank" (thana ʿitfahu) and "he turned away with his corner" (tawalla bi-ruknihi).

﴿And when evil touches him, then he is one of lengthy supplication﴾, i.e., abundant. It is borrowed from that which has a wide breadth (ʿarḍ mutta'si'), to indicate its abundance and continuity. It is more emphatic than "long" (ṭawil), since length is the longer of the two extensions; so if its breadth is like this, then what do you think of its length? Perhaps this is the condition of some, other than those of whom despair and hopelessness were reported, or it is the condition of all of them at some times.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 41, verse 52:

﴿Say: Have you considered?﴾ That is: inform me.

﴿If it is﴾ that is: the Qur'an.

﴿from Allah, and yet you disbelieve in it﴾ despite the mutually reinforcing reasons that necessitate belief in it.

﴿Who is further astray than one who is in extreme opposition?﴾ That is: who is further astray than you? The relative pronoun (al-mawsul, "the relative construction") has been placed in the position of the pronoun, to explain their condition and to give the reason for their greater misguidance.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 41, verse 53:**

﴿We will show them Our signs﴾ that indicate its reality and that it is from Allah.

﴿In the horizons﴾ refers to what the Prophet (ﷺ) informed them of regarding future events and the lasting effects of past calamities, and what Allah the Exalted will grant to him and to his successors of conquests and triumph over the horizons of the world, and the conquest of the lands of the East and the West in a manner that breaks custom.

﴿And within themselves﴾ refers to what appeared among the people of Makkah and what befell them. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him and his father) said: "In the horizons" means the dwelling places of the earlier nations and their traces, and "within themselves" means the Day of Badr. Mujahid, al-Hasan and al-Suddi said: "In the horizons" means what Allah opens of the towns for him (ﷺ) and the Muslims, and "within themselves" means the conquest of Makkah. It has also been said: "In the horizons" means in the regions of the heavens and the earth, from the sun, the moon and the stars, and what follows from them of night and day, light and shade, darkness, and from plants, trees and rivers. "And within themselves" means of the subtle craftsmanship and wondrous wisdom in the formation of embryos in the darkness of the wombs, and the emergence of the marvelous organs and the strange compositions, like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And within yourselves. Will you not see?﴾ It has been answered, regarding the particle of future (السين, sin), despite the fact that the showing of those signs had already taken place before that, that He, Exalted is He, will make them aware of those signs time after time and will increase them in understanding their realities day after day.

﴿Until it becomes clear to them﴾ through that.

﴿that it is the truth﴾, i.e., the Qur'an, or Islam and monotheism.

﴿Is it not sufficient with your Lord﴾: this is a resumptive sentence (استئناف, isti'naf) that comes to rebuke them for their hesitation concerning the matter of the Qur'an and their obstinacy, which necessitates the showing of signs, and for their not being content with His informing them, Exalted is He. The interrogative hamza (الهَمْزَةُ) is for denial, and the waw (الواوُ) is for coordination with an implied element required by the context, i.e., "Has your Lord not sufficed and not been enough?" The bi' (الباءُ) is additional for emphasis, and it is hardly ever added except with kafa (كفى). His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿that He is Witness over all things﴾ is a substitute (بدل, badal) for it, i.e., has it not sufficed them in place of the showing of the promised signs that clarify the reality of the Qur'an, and has it not been enough for them in this that He, Exalted is He, is Witness over all things, and He has informed that it is from Him?

It has also been said that its meaning is: this promised manifestation of the signs of Allah in the horizons and within themselves, they will see it and witness it, and at that time they will realize that the Qur'an is a revelation from the World of the Unseen, who is "Witness over all things," i.e., the All-Knowing, for whom His unseen and His seen are equal, and that this suffices them as proof that it is true and that it is from Him. Had it not been so, it would not have gained this strength, and its bearers would not have been granted this victory. So reflect.

As for what has been said, that the meaning is: "Is it not sufficient for you that He, Exalted is He, is Witness over all things, confirming it, so that He will confirm your affair by showing the promised signs just as He confirmed all the other promised things?" then, along with its implication of what is unbefitting the sublimity of his rank, peace be upon him, of hesitation regarding the confirmation of the promised matter mentioned, it is refuted by His saying, Exalted is He:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 41, verse 54:

﴿Ala inna-hum fi miryatin min liqa'i rabbi-him﴾ That is: in great doubt about that, namely the Resurrection and the recompense, for this is explicit that the lack of sufficiency is considered with respect to them. It is also read as "murya" with a ḍammah (ḍamm), and this is a dialect (lughah) of the word.

﴿Ala inna-hu bi-kulli shay'in muhit﴾ He is knowing of all things, their totalities and their details, their outward and their inward aspects, so that nothing of them is hidden from Him, and He will surely recompense them for their disbelief and their doubt. From the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surat al-Sajdah, God Most High will give him ten good deeds for every letter." And God knows best.
